# Quantization

Also called: Quantization with Matrix

## Overview
Quantization reduces the precision of volumetric data coefficients or raw values to decrease storage and memory bandwidth requirements. It sets itself apart from transform-based compression siblings by focusing on the discrete mapping of continuous values to a finite set of levels, often serving as the final lossy step before entropy encoding. Unlike [Value compression](6-value-compression.md) which encompasses the entire transform-encode pipeline, quantization specifically addresses the precision reduction mechanism.

## Shared principles
The family shares the mechanism of mapping a continuous or high-precision input domain to a discrete, lower-precision output domain. This process introduces quantization error, which is the difference between the original value and its quantized representation. The core trade-off is between the bit-rate (determined by the number of quantization levels) and the reconstruction fidelity. Methods vary in how they determine these levels (uniform, non-uniform, learned) and whether they operate on scalar values, vectors, or neural network parameters.

## Subtopics

### [Vector Quantization](907-vector-quantization.md)
Maps $n$-dimensional input vectors to a single fixed-length index referencing a codebook entry. It exploits spatial redundancy by grouping data blocks, enabling fast GPU decompression. Choose when spatial correlation within blocks is high and hardware-friendly lookup is required.

### [Scalar Quantization](5726-scalar-quantization.md)
Maps high-precision data to a lower-precision domain using local minimum and maximum values per block. It enables parallel, on-the-fly reconstruction in GPU-based direct volume rendering without full decompression. Choose for simple, hardware-friendly random access.

### [Chroma Subsampling](6512-chroma-subsampling.md)
Reduces chrominance resolution while maintaining full luminance resolution. It sets itself apart by defining one color value for every eight adjacent corners, preserving color quality better than direct subsampling. Choose for color volumetric data where luminance detail is critical.

### [Differentiable Quantization for Neural Fields](10195-differentiable-quantization-for-neural-fields.md)
Compresses neural field grid values to single bytes during optimization using a straight-through estimator. It solves quality degradation from naive post-training quantization. Choose for training neural radiance fields or Gaussian splatting with memory constraints.

### [Neural Implicit Network Compression](10414-neural-implicit-network-compression.md)
Compresses scientific volume data by training an Implicit Neural Representation (INR) with quantized weights. It enables direct querying of the implicit function, unlike traditional codecs that require full decoding. Choose for compact storage and queryable scientific data.

### [Unquantization Functions](13872-unquantization-functions.md)
Converts integer quantized values back to half-precision float range, specifically for BC6H compression. It differs from general scalar quantization by using scaling factors tailored to BC6H's partition structures. Choose for decompressing BC6H-compressed color volumes.

### [Global Quantization](15134-global-quantization.md)
Maintains a single shared parameter table across multiple independent MLPs within a neural volumetric representation. It solves redundancy by leveraging cross-MLP similarity. Choose for compressing large-scale neural volumetric representations with shared content patterns.

### Lossy Quantization for Coarsened Patches
Lossy compression for coarsened patches in a bintree hierarchy where quantization error $q$ is proportional to coarsening error $c$ ($q = qc$, with $q < 1$) [S2]. A single unified error is recomputed and nested for each patch. Quantization levels are restricted to power-of-two multiples of vertical resolution $\Delta z$ for efficient bit-shift implementation. The shift $k$ is calculated as $k = \lceil \log_2(\epsilon_q / \Delta z) \rceil + 1$ if $\epsilon_q \ge \Delta z$, else $0$. All finest level vertices have zero shift. Vertices are classified as boundary (corners $C$, legs $L$, hypotenuse $H$) and interior $I$. Corners are stored at full precision. Quantization of original height values (not residuals) ensures adjacent patches agree on shared boundaries [S2].

### HSV Colour Sorting
A technique to preserve colour quality during DXT1 compression by reordering colours based on HSV values [S3, unofficial]. The effectiveness depends on which component (H, S, or V) is the most frequent in the voxel data’s set of colours [S3, unofficial].

### Interpolation Symmetry Quantization
A method to improve the accuracy of quantized weights by exploiting the symmetry of linear interpolation between segments [S4]. Linear interpolation $(1 - w)s_i + w s_j$ is equivalent to $(j, i, 1 - w)$. The method quantizes both $w$ and $1 - w$ using the codebook generated by the scalar quantizer and keeps the representation resulting in the lower error. It stores either $(i, j, w)$ or $(j, i, 1 - w)$ in the output stream [S4].

### Position Lattice Quantization
An attempted method to compress Gaussian positions by quantizing them to a lattice structure and embedding positional constraints into the training process [S5]. It fails to compress positions without introducing significant rendering error [S5]. It is identified as a future research direction for end-to-end positional compression [S5].

### Post-finetune Refinement
A refinement step that uses a small number of bits to enhance the reconstruction quality of important voxels, compensating for losses introduced by coarse quantization [S6]. Ablation study on Synthetic-NeRF dataset shows disabling post-finetune causes a -1.72 dB $\Delta$PSNR, -0.07 $\Delta$SSIM, and -0.079 MB $\Delta$Size [S6]. Disabling post-finetune saves bits but inevitably deteriorates rendering quality, confirming its necessity for maintaining RD performance [S6].

## Background
Quantization is a fundamental technique in data compression, widely used in image and video coding standards (e.g., JPEG, MPEG) and increasingly in neural network compression. In volume rendering, it is often applied to transform coefficients (DCT, Wavelet) or raw voxel values to reduce memory footprint. The specific application to neural radiance fields and implicit representations is a recent development, driven by the need to store large grid-based or network-based representations efficiently.
